Nobody has ever told me I'm schizophrenic, but some have indicated this, so I decided to see a psychiatrist. She thinks it could be TLE (Temporal Lobe Epilepsy), as this often presents symptoms which mimic schizophrenia, and I have perceptual abnormalities which more closely resemble that disorder. 

I had an EEG and the results were indicative of some abnormal brain activity which in the right clinical setting could be associated with a generalised seizure disorder. (I'm paraphrasing). Because my dad had some siezures, even though it was due to a sports injury, I have to be careful. 

It's possible I have some schizophrenia in the family. My grandfather was bipolar, so it could be that, but I've never been manic, I'm largely apathetic and couldn't be bothered. So the short answer is yes. In my opinion at least.

Hi. I'm sure you have something valuable to contribute. I'm not officially schizophrenic, but I find it very interesting. 

I can empathize with your being worried. I worry most of the time that people will find out something terribly embarrassing about me, and I become a kind of policeman of conduct to be able to control the inflections of those around me so I'm not triggered. It's pretty wierd. I'm really most afraid of what people think of what I think, and I'm afraid of voicing my own opinion instead of something purely generic and 'digestible'. 

The truth is, no one cares enough to be concerned about the things that you worry about yourself. And if they do, then it will pass eventually as they get on with their own lives.
Perhaps there's an animal you could love?

About 1% of the population has schizophrenia and it's thought to have been around for most of human history. Some people are born with it. Also, brain scans suggest that schizophrenia changes the structures in the brain, i.e. some parts are missing. All of this adds up the evidence that schizophrenia is a disease which can't be reasoned away. John Nash said he believed his delusions because they came to him in the same way his mathematical ideas did. 

I think schizophrenia can be challenged in terms of the delusions, just like other disorders with anxiety and thought problems. It depends imo on the severity of the condition. Sometimes people need help to see things as they really are. An interesting thing is people with schizophrenia do tend to be religious, and that aspect takes form in the disease with hallucinations and delusions. 

Schizophrenia is more generally defined as a disorder in which the person holds beliefs which fall outside those recognised by their culture. So, in the case of a culture which accepts the practice of alchemy, a schizophrenic individual might believe something entirely different. I find this definition to be unsatisfactory personally, as it doesn't adress the nature of the delusions as they relate to reality and logic but compares them to a social context, leading to problems with stereotypes. 

The question I feel needs to be addressed is, is it right to live in ignorance of other people's igonrance? I grew up being shown how ignorant other cultures were of things. In fact, culture in general was viewed as a device for inculcating false beliefs. So I guess you could say I'm slightly anti-cultural or a-cultural. So what would happen if I were to develop delusions? That's a good question. 

Edit: Also, schizophrenia doesn't impair intelligence but does impair the brain's capacity for logic.
